resources.string: This app is designed to provide communication during disasters. To continue, you must indicate that you have read and accepted the terms below.
I have read it all and I accept it.
Connecting lives when it matters most
Crisis Connect can also send messages over the internet — encrypted and using very little data, so it keeps working when networks are congested.
Messages are tiny and delivered over the OS push channel, so they get through even on weak connections.
Far fewer connections and retries means less load on base stations during a disaster.
Only you and the recipient can read the message — the server never sees the content.
So contacts who know your number can reach you over the internet.

Phone speakers are hardware-limited. The app targets the most noticeable output using the alarm stream, rescue-band tuning, and extra gain when supported.
The 2-4 kHz range is easier for human hearing to pick up; rescue modes sweep through this band.
Higher power and boost can cut through noise better, but increase battery use and heat.
An external audio device is active. Disconnect headphones or Bluetooth for the strongest outward alert.

The whistle can be very loud. If you continue, the app may temporarily raise the alarm stream to maximum. Keep the phone away from your ears.
If possible, position the phone near doors, windows, or openings.
Use it in intervals and avoid running at full power for too long in confined spaces.
If you are trapped, use interval whistle bursts together with tapping on pipes or walls and short messages instead of shouting continuously.
The digital whistle opens in Continuous mode by default. You can fine-tune the center frequency, switch playback modes, and adjust output presets while it plays.

Continuous gives an uninterrupted alert. Pulse fires short bursts to grab attention. SOS repeats the classic "··· --- ···" pattern. Siren Sweep moves frequency up and down. Rescue mode alternates multiple tones in the 2-4 kHz band for better cut-through on phone speakers.
Keep the phone speaker away from ears. The app may temporarily max the alarm stream and apply extra gain when supported, so use intervals in confined areas and mute as soon as contact is made.

Your phone’s magnetometer reacts strongly to ferromagnetic metals such as iron or steel. Non-ferromagnetic metals like gold, silver, or copper produce little or no response.
Earth’s magnetic field is normally 30–60 µT. Nearby speakers, chargers, or cases may cause spikes, so step away from electronics before scanning.
